The power went out at eleven, the night before the accounts exam, and the hostel generator coughed and died. Ankita and Jyoti gave up revising by phone torch and lay on their beds in the dark.
"Can I tell you something?" Ankita said. "My parents barely speak now. Papa sleeps at the shop some nights." She waited, heart loud, for Jyoti to change the subject.
Jyoti didn't. "That sounds so lonely for you," she said. After a pause: "I'm scared I'll fail this course and my mother will say she knew it." Then, quieter: "And I still check my ex's profile. Two years later. Pathetic."
"Not pathetic," Ankita said. "I did the same with mine for a whole summer."
When the lights came back at one, neither of them reached for their notes straight away. They'd have to cram at dawn, but it felt as if they'd both passed a test they hadn't studied for.

qa.q: When did the lights come back?
qa.a: The lights came back at one.

qa.q: Why did Ankita wait with her heart loud after speaking?
qa.a: Ankita was afraid Jyoti might change the subject; she was checking whether Jyoti would respond with care.

qa.q: What made this conversation deepen the friendship?
qa.a: Each disclosure was met with care and matched: Jyoti named Ankita's loneliness and shared her own fears, and Ankita answered 'Not pathetic' with a story of her own. 🤍

qa.q: What would change if Jyoti had changed the subject?
qa.a: Ankita would likely feel exposed and pull back, and the friendship might have stayed on the surface instead of becoming real.

grounding: Shows two hostel friends trading family troubles, career fears and old heartbreak, each watching whether the other responds with care.

The bakery near the college gate in Hyderabad was nearly empty at four. Rehana stirred her tea for too long before she said it: her engagement had been called off in the summer, and her khala still brought it up at every family dinner.
Jyoti put down her puff. She'd known Rehana for five months, mostly as a lab partner. For a second she didn't know what to say, then chose honesty. "I didn't know. I'm sorry. That must feel like it's on display all the time."
Rehana nodded, eyes on the cup.
Jyoti took a breath. "Can I tell you mine? I'm terrified I won't get placed. Papa's shop closed in March and everyone's counting on me."
Rehana looked up properly then. "You carry that into lab every day, alone?"
They stayed till the owner started stacking chairs. On the walk to the bus stop, Jyoti kept thinking: she told me first, and she didn't flinch at mine.

qa.q: What did Rehana share about the summer?
qa.a: Rehana said her engagement had been called off in the summer.

qa.q: What was Jyoti thinking on the walk to the bus stop?
qa.a: Jyoti felt trusted and safe: Rehana had told her first and didn't flinch at her fears, so the friendship now felt real.

qa.q: How did Jyoti respond in a way that helped Rehana trust her?
qa.a: Jyoti named how exposed Rehana must feel instead of giving advice, then shared a fear of her own, so the openness went both ways.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when Jyoti shared her placement fear?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt less alone and more trusted, and saw that Jyoti thought of her as a real friend, not just a lab partner.

grounding: Illustrates two young women deepening a friendship through matched disclosures about heartbreak, family pressure and career fear, each checking for care.

It was past midnight on the roof of their rented flat in Hyderabad when Siddharth said, out of nowhere, "My parents haven't spoken to each other properly in two years."

Nitin put down his tea. They had shared the flat for four months, cooked together, argued about cricket, but never this.

Siddharth kept going: the silent dinners, how he used to invent reasons to stay late at college, how he dreaded going home for Diwali.

Nitin listened without interrupting. When Siddharth stopped, Nitin was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "I failed my first engineering exam. I still haven't told my father. I'm scared I'm not cut out for this."

Siddharth turned to look at him. "Seriously? You?"

"Seriously."

Neither of them offered advice. They just sat there until the city lights started going off, knowing something had changed between them.

qa.q: How long had Nitin and Siddharth shared the flat?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: Why does Nitin share his own failed exam after listening?
qa.a: He feels trusted by Siddharth's honesty and wants to answer with care and his own openness, even though he is scared about not being cut out for engineering.

qa.q: What worked well in how they responded to each other?
qa.a: Each listened without interrupting or rushing to give advice, and answered one disclosure with another, which made both feel safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth to hear Nitin's fear?
qa.a: He is surprised, since Nitin seemed confident, and probably relieved that his own trouble was met with trust rather than awkwardness.

grounding: Nitin and Siddharth trade family troubles and career fears late at night, and each responds with care, showing reciprocal disclosure making the friendship real.

"Can I tell you something weird, Akash?"

"Weirder than you eating mango with salt?"

"Shut up. Seriously."

"Okay. Serious face. Go."

"I don't actually want to be a CA. My dad picked it. I'm doing the course because saying no would break his heart."

"...Chinmay. That's not weird. That's huge."

"You won't tell anyone?"

"Who would I tell? My cat?"

"You're laughing."

"I'm not laughing at you. Okay. Can I tell you mine?"

"Go."

"I got dumped in March. By text. I still read the messages sometimes."

"That's why you disappeared that month."

"Yeah."

"Man. I thought you were just studying."

"I was pretending to study."

"Okay. So now we both know stuff."

"Now we both know stuff. That's scary."

"Kind of nice, though."

qa.a: By text.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's question "You won't tell anyone?" show about how he feels?

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage, and how do they use it?
qa.a: When one shares, the other can answer with care and share too; Akash does this by sharing his breakup, making the exchange mutual.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to feel about finally telling Chinmay about March?
qa.a: He probably feels a little embarrassed but relieved, since the lonely month now makes sense to his friend.

passage:
I remember the exact evening Jatin and I became real friends, not just classmates who shared notes.

We were sitting on the steps outside the library after an exam that went badly for both of us. I said, half joking, that if I failed again my mother would stop introducing me as her daughter the doctor.

Jatin didn't laugh. He said, "My brother dropped out last year. My parents still don't say his name at dinner."

We sat with that for a while. Then I told him the thing I hadn't told anyone, about the boy from school who left without a word, and how I still check his page some nights.

Jatin didn't judge. He just nodded and said, "That sounds lonely."

I watched him closely as I said it, I admit. I was checking whether he'd make it a joke. He didn't.

— Avni

qa.q: Where were Avni and Jatin sitting that evening?
qa.a: On the steps outside the library after an exam.

qa.q: Why was Avni watching Jatin so closely while sharing?
qa.a: Avni was nervous and vulnerable, checking whether Jatin would turn the disclosure into a joke or respond with care.

qa.q: What did Jatin do that helped the friendship grow?
qa.a: He shared something painful about his own family and then answered Avni's secret without judging, simply saying it sounded lonely.

qa.q: How might Jatin have felt telling Avni about his brother?
qa.a: He may have felt anxious and sad, since his parents don't even say his brother's name, but also trusting that Avni would care.

grounding: Avni and Jatin swap family pressures and an old heartbreak, each checking the other responds with care, which turns classmates into real friends.

passage:
Buddy programme note, first-year hostel, week 6. Written by the student mentor coordinator.

Pairing Hansa and Gargi appears to be working. At the start, both mostly talked about classes. In today's check-in, they asked to meet me together.

Gargi said she had told Hansa about her parents' separation, which no one else at college knows. She said she'd watched Hansa's face "to see if she'd pity me or judge me." Hansa didn't do either; she just said, "That sounds lonely," and then told Gargi about her own fear of failing and letting her father down.

Hansa said that after that night, she felt "like I had a person here."

I noticed how carefully each watched the other while telling their story. That seems to be what they were really testing: whether it was safe.

No action needed. Will continue fortnightly check-ins.

qa.q: What did Hansa say after Gargi shared about her parents?
qa.a: Hansa said, "That sounds lonely."

qa.q: What was Gargi afraid of when telling Hansa about the separation?
qa.a: Gargi was afraid Hansa would pity or judge her, so she watched Hansa's face closely.

qa.q: Why did Hansa's response help the friendship deepen?
qa.a: She responded with care and then shared her own fear, which made the disclosure mutual and showed it was safe.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after that night?
qa.a: Hansa felt she finally had someone at college, a sense of belonging and trust.

grounding: A mentor's note shows two new friends sharing family troubles and fears in turn, each checking whether the other responds with care.
